title: fragmentation-entropy-allocator-observations
content:
Summary:

This note captures a set of experiments, observations, and mitigation ideas carried out to investigate repeated OOMs in a multi-tenant serving cluster. The angle here is intentionally different: rather than only tracking peak bytes allocated, we instrumented the allocator to measure a lightweight fragmentation metric we call 'fragmentation entropy' and used it to correlate allocation patterns, cudaMallocAsync behavior, and long-lived workspace usage.

Background / Context:
- Symptoms: intermittent OOMs on P40/V100/RTX hosts during high-concurrency inference workloads; OOMs appeared even when aggregate live memory (sum of tensor sizes) was well under device capacity.
- Hypothesis before this work: peak working set spikes and poor batching were primary causes. After initial traces, we saw strong evidence that internal fragmentation and allocator metadata/misaligned blocks were causing unusable free space pockets.
- Goals: (1) characterize allocator-level fragmentation over time, (2) identify allocator operations that exacerbate fragmentation (cudaMalloc, cudaFree, cudaMallocAsync, cudaMemPool*), and (3) propose pragmatic mitigations for serving runtime.

What we added / tools we used:
- Small shim layer around our in-house allocator that records allocation size, timestamp, stream id, and arena id to a lightweight log (binary + small JSON summaries).
- NVTX markers at model boundary and workspace alloc/free paths.
- periodic snapshots of OS-visible device memory with nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -lms 2000 (coarse but useful to correlate).
- Used cudaMallocAsync and cudaMemPool APIs where possible; toggled between default cudaMallocAsync (CUDA 11/12 behaviour) and fallbacks to cudaMalloc to measure differences.
- A simple 'entropy' metric computed on the free-list histogram (bucket free block counts by power-of-two size, compute normalized distribution p_i and entropy H = -sum p_i log2 p_i). The idea: higher entropy -> more evenly distributed small free blocks -> worse packing for large allocations.

Key observations (ordered roughly by impact):
1) Divergent lifetime classes drive entropy growth: short-lived per-request buffers (few KB–MB) interleaved with long-lived KV caches and persistent model activations produce a bimodal free-block distribution. When long-lived blocks are freed (rare), leftover holes are frequently too small for trailing large workspace allocations. Entropy rises across the timeline and correlates with OOM windows.

2) cudaMallocAsync reduces wall-clock latency but can delay coalescing: cuMallocAsync keeps freed blocks in per-stream pools and only returns them to the global pool on stream synchronization or pool trim. On high-concurrency with many streams, we observed many small per-stream pools holding onto pieces that would otherwise be reusable, increasing fragmentation entropy. Turning off cudaMallocAsync reduced entropy (and slightly increased allocation latency) but prevented a class of OOMs.

3) Allocation alignment and padding: our allocator rounds up to 256B for alignment; large numbers of 256B to 4KB allocations cause internal slop. More importantly, some CUDA runtime allocations we don't control request 64B alignments and are rounded externally, amplifying small-block churn. Changing internal alignment to prefer 4KB slabs for small short-lived buffers dramatically lowered entropy in microbenchmarks.

4) Per-model arena isolation helps: colocating short-lived per-request workspaces into transient arenas that can be retired/trimmed as a unit reduced entropy growth. Retiring an arena is faster than trying to defragment global free lists. However, per-model arenas increase peak reserved memory if not carefully sized.

5) cudaMemPoolTrimTo and mempool attributes: on CUDA versions supporting mempool trimming, calling cudaMemPoolTrimTo with an encouraged size during quiet periods helped return memory to the device global pool and reduced entropy. But frequent trimming had its own cost (extra PCIe activity and higher latency for the first subsequent allocation).

6) Time-of-use packing window: we introduced a sliding packing window heuristic that attempts to reuse recently-freed blocks for allocations that arrive within a short temporal window (ms scale). It works well for workloads with high temporal locality (same request reusing buffer sizes) and lowered entropy and failure rate in our latency-sensitive path.

Experimental repro steps (short):
1) Build tiny reproducer: a workload that alternates between: (A) allocate a long-lived 200–300MB KV cache tensor per model; (B) perform 200 concurrent requests that allocate many small (~64KB–2MB) per-request buffers and free them; (C) allocate a large workspace (~1.5GB) for attention/cache growth.
2) Run two variants: allocator with cudaMallocAsync enabled vs disabled; recorder enabled to capture per-op logs.
3) Collect free-list histograms every 100ms and compute entropy. Capture NVTX and nvidia-smi.

Representative command snippets we used:
- python reproducible_load.py --concurrency 200 --kv-size 250MB --workspace 1.5GB
- nvprof / nvtx traces collected via our internal trace wrapper
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -lms 2000 > memlog.csv &

Measured signals to watch (examples):
- Entropy H over time (plot with peak H preceding OOMs)
- Number of per-stream free chunks held (cudaMallocAsync)
- Longest contiguous free span reported by allocator (we added a fast pass to compute this)
- Allocation latency distribution when grabbing large contiguous spans

Concrete root causes identified:
- Mixed size allocations with skewed lifetimes created many small pockets unusable for large workspace allocations. The allocator's first-fit-with-coalescing strategy could not coalesce across pooled per-stream caches until sync/trim.
- cudaMallocAsync's pooling semantics interact poorly with our per-request concurrency pattern (many streams), producing a hidden 'held' free memory that is usable only after stream sync/trim.
- Default mempool parameters left small block buckets under-provisioned; pressure would cause growth in many tiny buckets rather than compacting into larger reusable spans.

Mitigations we validated (ranked):
1) Short term (low-risk): disable cudaMallocAsync for the serving process group that experiences heavy stream concurrency. This immediately reduced observed entropy and eliminated a class of OOMs in canaries at the cost of minor increase in tail allocation latency.
2) Medium term (allocator changes): implement per-request transient arenas (recyclable slab pools) for small buffers and pack them by bucketed slab sizes. Retire arena on model unload / quiet window. This reduced small-block churn and entropy by ~40% in our tests.
3) Medium term (CUDA features): if available, tune cudaMemPoolSetAttribute to set lower per-stream retention thresholds and call cudaMemPoolTrimTo during quieter intervals between request bursts. Test carefully — trimming can increase p99 latency for first allocation after a trim.
4) Long term (placement/strategy): introduce an online fragmentation entropy metric to the runtime metrics dashboard; when entropy exceeds a threshold, trigger adaptive actions: (a) switch off async pooling; (b) opportunistically evict/compact KV cache entries; (c) start a controlled arena retirement cycle.
5) Operational: add a 'workspace emergency' fallback: if a large contiguous allocation fails, fall back to a multi-chunk planner that maps the logical workspace across several smaller allocations and uses chunked kernel paths (slower but avoids complete failure). Requires kernel-level support for split KV/attn buffers.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Turning off cudaMallocAsync vs trimming means trading steady-state latency vs memory availability. Different customer tiers (dedicated vs hosted) might prefer different defaults.
- How aggressive should arena retirement be? Too aggressive = wasted peak reservation; too passive = fragmentation persists. Need a cost model per model: expected request volume vs cost of reserve.
- Can we upstream a simple entropy diagnostic to CUDA mempools? We currently compute H from our own free-list histograms. A standardized mempool API exposing large-contiguous-span size would be ideal.

Next steps / action items:
- (Sergio) Run wider fleet canary with cudaMallocAsync disabled for high-concurrency instance types for 2 weeks and report regressions. (ETA: 2 weeks)
- (Ethan) Prototype transient per-request arenas in the allocator: simple bucketed slabs + retire API. Measure p50/p95/p99 latency impact and memory reduction. (ETA: 3 weeks)
- (Priya) Add fragmentation entropy chart to Redwood Console dashboards and set alerting threshold (start with H > 2.0 based on current normalization). (ETA: 1 week)
- (Maya) Draft operational runbook describing emergency fallback behavior when contiguous workspace allocation fails (chunked planner + runtime switch). (ETA: 1 week)

Appendix: quick pseudo-algorithms used
- Entropy computation (very lightweight):
  1. bucketize free-list by power-of-two sizes (e.g., 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, ... up to big buckets).
  2. compute counts c_i and normalize p_i = c_i / sum c_i.
  3. H = -sum p_i * log2(p_i). Report H in metric pipeline along with max_free_span.

- Arena retire heuristic (simplified):
  if arena.last_used_ts + quiet_window_ms < now and arena.utilization < threshold:
    mark arena for retire
    migrate outstanding long-lived tensors (if any) or reject new model loads into that arena
    free arena back to global pool via mempool trim call

Notes about uniqueness of this doc: focuses on entropy as a diagnostic and operational response curves, mixes allocator engineering with product-level fallback strategies and dashboarding ideas. The language intentionally avoids repeating prior filenames and centers on heuristics rather than low-level allocator heap walkthroughs.

End of note.
